title: Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc “You Can See Everything” Premieres in New York, No Longer a Secret
body:
The much‑anticipated documentary “You Can See Everything,” co‑directed by comedian‑filmmaker Nathan Fielder and writer‑producer Lance Oppenheim, finally shed its veil of secrecy when it debuted at the New York Film Festival on Wednesday. The film, which chronicles the meteoric rise and spectacular fall of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, offers a surreal, almost hyper‑real portrait of a saga that has already been dissected in books, podcasts and courtroom drama. Its premiere marks the first public screening of a project that has been whispered about in industry circles for months, and it signals a new chapter in the cultural reckoning with one of the most infamous corporate frauds of the 21st century.

The documentary’s title—“You Can See Everything”—is both a literal nod to the surveillance‑style footage that permeates the film and a sardonic comment on the illusion of transparency that Holmes once sold to investors, patients and the media. Fielder, best known for his dead‑pan mock‑reality series “Nathan for You,” brings his trademark off‑kilter sensibility to the material, blending archival news clips, courtroom recordings, and newly shot interviews with a cast of insiders who range from former Theranos employees to journalists who chased the story. The result is a collage that feels part investigative report, part performance art, and part dark comedy, leaving viewers to question how much of the narrative is constructed and how much is pure fact.

Critics who have seen the film describe it as a “strange, hard‑to‑believe coda” to a saga that already reads like a cautionary novel. While earlier accounts, such as the bestselling book *Bad Blood* and the popular podcast *The Dropout*, focused on the mechanics of the fraud—falsified test results, a culture of intimidation, and the eventual criminal convictions—the documentary leans into the mythic dimensions of Holmes herself. It portrays her as a modern‑day alchemist, a charismatic figure who convinced Silicon Valley’s elite to invest in a vision of blood‑testing that never existed. Yet the film also refuses to romanticize; it juxtaposes her polished public persona with footage of her nervous demeanor during the 2021 trial, underscoring the human cost of the deception.

The timing of the premiere is significant. Holmes’ sentencing in November 2022—four years in prison and a $452 million restitution order—has long been a focal point for discussions about accountability in the tech sector. By releasing the documentary at a high‑profile festival, the filmmakers position the story within a broader cultural conversation about the perils of “fake it till you make it” mentalities that pervade startup culture. In an era where venture capital can turn a fledgling idea into a multi‑billion‑dollar valuation overnight, “You Can See Everything” serves as a stark reminder that unchecked hype can have real, harmful consequences for patients, investors and employees alike.

Industry observers note that the film’s unconventional style may limit its mainstream appeal but could also attract a niche audience eager for a fresh perspective on a well‑trodden narrative. The documentary’s blend of humor and horror reflects a growing trend in nonfiction storytelling that blurs the line between reportage and art. As streaming platforms scramble for exclusive content, the documentary’s eventual distribution—whether through a limited theatrical run, a streaming service or a combination of both—will likely influence how the Theranos story is remembered by future generations.

Looking ahead, “You Can See Everything” may prompt renewed scrutiny of regulatory frameworks governing health‑tech startups and inspire more rigorous journalistic investigations into Silicon Valley’s most audacious promises. Whether it reshapes public perception of Elizabeth Holmes or simply adds another layer to an already complex tale, the documentary’s arrival at the New York Film Festival confirms that the conversation about Theranos is far from over. As audiences leave the theater, they are left with a lingering question: in an age of ubiquitous surveillance and curated narratives, can we ever truly see everything?
